headline: PSPA to install 252 new filtration plants, restore 59 non-functional units in Rawalpindi
description: RAWALPINDI - Deputy Commissioner Rawalpindi, Captain (Retd) Nadeem Nasir here on Tuesday chaired a meeting at his office to review the progress of
author: OUR STAFF REPORT
article_text:
RAWALPINDI - Deputy Commissioner Rawalpindi, Captain (Retd) Nadeem Nasir here on Tuesday chaired a meeting at his office to review the progress of ongoing projects under the Punjab Saaf Pani Authority (PSPA), focusing on the rehabilitation of non-functional water filtration plants and the installation of new ones across the district.

The meeting was attended by Additional Deputy Commissioner (Municipal Services) Junaid Alam, assistant commissioners, managing director WA SA, and other concerned officials.

During the session, officials were given a comprehensive briefing regarding the authority’s initiatives. Out of the 241 existing water filtration plants in Rawalpindi district, 182 are currently operational.

The rehabilitation of the remaining 59 non-functional plants is underway through the Frontier Works Organization (FWO), with a completion deadline set for November 30, 2026.

The meeting was further informed that under Phase-I of the Chief Minister Punjab Saaf Pani Program, 252 new water filtration plants are being installed across five tehsils of the district at a cost of Rs1.47 billion. Work has commenced on 187 out of 205 handed-over sites, with 65 filtration plants already installed.

Stressing the importance of quality, speed, and timely completion, DC Nadeem Nasir directed the officials to accelerate the installation and restoration work to ensure clean drinking water for citizens. He instructed all assistant commissioners to submit a complete progress report by coming Saturday.

He also ordered regular monitoring of operational plants, water quality testing, and an efficient operation and maintenance system to maintain uninterrupted supply. Additionally, the meeting highlighted the need for a robust digital monitoring mechanism and prompt grievance redressal for local residents.

headline: PTI–JUI-F rapprochement: little likelihood of a grand opposition alliance
description: ISLAMABAD - As JUI-F chief Maulana Fazlur Rehman intensifies his criticism of the federal government and security establishment, opposition
author: Imran Mukhtar
article_text:
ISLAMABAD - As JUI-F chief Maulana Fazlur Rehman intensifies his criticism of the federal government and security establishment, opposition alliance TTAP is looking towards him to spearhead a broader anti-government movement.

This raises a key question: can two longstanding political rivals, the Jamiat Ulema-i-Islam-Fazl (JUI-F) and the Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI), agree on a common agenda for a grand opposition alliance and to run a movement?

The opposition alliance Tehreek-i-Tahafuz-i-Ayin-i-Pakistan (TTAP) has recently unveiled plans to start an anti-government campaign with its spokesperson Hussain Ahmed Yousufzai in a statement saying that Maulana will likely lead it.

The latest PTI-JUI-F rapprochement started in mid-October when Mauala severely criticized the federal government for imposing an emergency and governor’s rule in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa—the steps that had made Imran Khan’s party-led provincial government dysfunctional. He also accused the Pakistan Muslim League-Nawaz (PML-N)-led government for derailing the talks process with the PTI by backing out its commitments despite his mediation efforts.

On October 4, the PTI-dominated TTAP had gathered at the residence of JUI-F chief in Islamabad where all parties agreed to strengthen their alliance. Following the statement of the opposition alliance’s spokesperson, it is quite evident that the TTAP leadership including National Assembly opposition leader Mehmood Khan Achakzai and Leader of the Opposition in the Senate Raja Nasir Abbas are looking towards firebrand Maulana to lead the anti-government movement. Contrary to this, there are very slim chances that the PTI as a party agrees to sit with the JUI-F due to multiple reasons.

According to a senior politician belonging to the party of Imran Khan, the JUI-F and the PTI despite being in opposition are standing in opposite directions. While Maulana heaps on his anti-government and anti-establishment campaign, the present leadership of the PTI has adopted a different tone even after the party lost its government in KP. Interim PTI Chairman Gohar Ali Khan always avoids taking a harsh line against his opponents and adopts the policy of reconciliation. With this strategy, he is trying to find a way out to lessen present troubles for his party. The leadership has even disassociated itself with the official X handles of PTI and Imran Khan who have been using critical language against opponents.

With growing concerns within opposition circles that the JUI-F would meet a similar fate as PTI, the latter is keen to prevent the party from being subjected to the same harsh treatment it had experienced in the past. Legal counsel Salman Safdar’s meeting with incarcerated PTI founder Imran Khan and his wife Bushra Bibi after a gap of months is being seen as a ray of hope and the PTI leadership wants to get some more relief through its conciliatory tone. A PTI insider said that all tiers of the party have been instructed by the top leadership to share video statements on social media, appealing to powers-that-be that Khan should get his due rights in jail and treatment from a choice of his hospital in the presence of his personal physicians. This indicates that the party is in no mood of confrontation.

The PTI looks at the present TTAP leadership with suspicion, accusing Achakzai that he has failed to serve the purpose for which he had been nominated the opposition leader by Khan. He is being criticized within the party circles not only for his alleged failure to engage with the government but also for not giving an effective protest strategy.

Against this backdrop, there is little likelihood that the PTI will endorse TTAP’s proposal to have Maulana Fazlur Rehman lead an anti-government movement. While one faction of the party, led by Asad Qaiser, may welcome the proposal, a significant section within the PTI including those aligned with Ali Amin Gandapur is likely to oppose it, given the longstanding rivalry between Gandapur and the JUI-F chief.

More broadly, the PTI is unlikely to concede political space to the JUI-F in KP, where the two parties compete for the same constituencies. article_html:
ISLAMABAD  -  As JUI-F chief Maulana Fazlur Rehman intensifies his criticism of the federal government and security establishment, opposition alliance TTAP is looking towards him to spearhead a broader anti-government movement.

This raises a key question: can two longstanding political rivals, the Jamiat Ulema-i-Islam-Fazl (JUI-F) and the Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI), agree on a common agenda for a grand opposition alliance and to run a movement?

The opposition alliance Tehreek-i-Tahafuz-i-Ayin-i-Pakistan (TTAP) has recently unveiled plans to start an anti-government campaign with its spokesperson Hussain Ahmed Yousufzai in a statement saying that Maulana will likely lead it.

ATC grants 13-day remand of 2 JUI-F men; party alleges harassment

The latest PTI-JUI-F rapprochement started in mid-October when Mauala severely criticized the federal government for imposing an emergency and governor’s rule in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa—the steps that had made Imran Khan’s party-led provincial government dysfunctional.  He also accused the Pakistan Muslim League-Nawaz (PML-N)-led government for derailing the talks process with the PTI by backing out its commitments despite his mediation efforts.

On October 4, the PTI-dominated TTAP had gathered at the residence of JUI-F chief in Islamabad where all parties agreed to strengthen their alliance. Following the statement of the opposition alliance’s spokesperson, it is quite evident that the TTAP leadership including National Assembly opposition leader Mehmood Khan Achakzai and Leader of the Opposition in the Senate Raja Nasir Abbas are looking towards firebrand Maulana to lead the anti-government movement. Contrary to this, there are very slim chances that the PTI as a party agrees to sit with the JUI-F due to multiple reasons.

Court rejects plea to drop terrorism charge in Group Captain’s murder case

According to a senior politician belonging to the party of Imran Khan, the JUI-F and the PTI despite being in opposition are standing in opposite directions. While Maulana heaps on his anti-government and anti-establishment campaign, the present leadership of the PTI has adopted a different tone even after the party lost its government in KP. Interim PTI Chairman Gohar Ali Khan always avoids taking a harsh line against his opponents and adopts the policy of reconciliation. With this strategy, he is trying to find a way out to lessen present troubles for his party. The leadership has even disassociated itself with the official X handles of PTI and Imran Khan who have been using critical language against opponents.

Senate Health Committee calls for strict enforcement of breastfeeding ordinance

With growing concerns within opposition circles that the JUI-F would meet a similar fate as PTI, the latter is keen to prevent the party from being subjected to the same harsh treatment it had experienced in the past. Legal counsel Salman Safdar’s meeting with incarcerated PTI founder Imran Khan and his wife Bushra Bibi after a gap of months is being seen as a ray of hope and the PTI leadership wants to get some more relief through its conciliatory tone. A PTI insider said that all tiers of the party have been instructed by the top leadership to share video statements on social media, appealing to powers-that-be that Khan should get his due rights in jail and treatment from a choice of his hospital in the presence of his personal physicians. This indicates that the party is in no mood of confrontation.

5 stolen motorcycles recovered in police crackdown in Kahuta

The PTI looks at the present TTAP leadership with suspicion, accusing Achakzai that he has failed to serve the purpose for which he had been nominated the opposition leader by Khan. He is being criticized within the party circles not only for his alleged failure to engage with the government but also for not giving an effective protest strategy.

Against this backdrop, there is little likelihood that the PTI will endorse TTAP’s proposal to have Maulana Fazlur Rehman lead an anti-government movement. While one faction of the party, led by Asad Qaiser, may welcome the proposal, a significant section within the PTI including those aligned with Ali Amin Gandapur is likely to oppose it, given the longstanding rivalry between Gandapur and the JUI-F chief.

RWU holds 4th BASR meeting, reviews PhD, MPhil research synopses

More broadly, the PTI is unlikely to concede political space to the JUI-F in KP, where the two parties compete for the same constituencies. Maulana’s increasing rhetoric against the establishment can also be viewed in the context of JUI-F’s efforts to regain political ground and expand its influence in the province.

ENDs/

headline: Past in Perspective
description: The Partition of Palestine in 1947 was a UN resolution to divide British-controlled Palestine into separate Jewish and Arab states. While accepted by Jewish
author: The Nation
article_text: The Partition of Palestine in 1947 was a UN resolution to divide British-controlled Palestine into separate Jewish and Arab states. While accepted by Jewish leaders, Arab nations rejected the plan for several reasons, leading to conflict. This partition marked a crucial moment in the Israeli-Palestinian conflict, laying the groundwork for the establishment of the State of Israel in 1948 and the displacement of hundreds of thousands of Palestinians. The unresolved tensions from this event continue to shape the region’s political landscape to this day, fueling ongoing violence and diplomatic disputes. As we watch the genocide unfold in Gaza, it is eye-opening to remember the disparity with which this entire conflict began.

headline: AI Reliance and Critical Thinking
description: Artificial intelligence has made academic work faster and more convenient, but excessive reliance on it risks weakening students’ ability to think
author: The Nation
article_text:
Artificial intelligence has made academic work faster and more convenient, but excessive reliance on it risks weakening students’ ability to think independently. Many university students now turn to AI chatbots for ready-made answers, summaries and essays instead of reading, researching and developing their own arguments.

When students stop analysing information independently, their problem-solving abilities and creativity can suffer. AI should be a learning aid, not a replacement for independent thinking. Universities and colleges should introduce assignments that encourage classroom discussions, presentations and original writing. Students must learn to use technology responsibly while developing the critical thinking skills essential for their future.

BATOOL FATIMA,

Karachi.

headline: Iqbal’s Vision
description: Allama Muhammad Iqbal, the Poet of the East and one of the intellectual architects of Pakistan, awakened a nation through his poetry and philosophy, inspiring
author: The Nation
article_text:
Allama Muhammad Iqbal, the Poet of the East and one of the intellectual architects of Pakistan, awakened a nation through his poetry and philosophy, inspiring generations to embrace self-respect, faith, knowledge, freedom and purposeful action.

Iqbal’s vision extended beyond poetry. His philosophy of Khudi (selfhood) urged individuals to recognise their inner strength, develop independent thought and rise above fear and complacency. His ideas also strengthened political consciousness and a distinct national identity among the Muslims of the subcontinent, contributing significantly to the intellectual foundations of the Pakistan Movement.

Although Iqbal did not live to witness Pakistan’s creation in 1947, his vision continues to inspire us to build a nation founded on knowledge, dignity, justice and intellectual freedom.

His message to young people remains particularly relevant. Through the symbol of the Shaheen (falcon), Iqbal envisioned a generation that soars high, confronts challenges courageously, rejects blind imitation, and charts its own course. He believed that young people are not merely the future of a nation; they have the power to transform its present.

Today, Pakistan needs more than admiration for Iqbal’s poetry. It needs the practical application of his teachings in educational institutions, public leadership, and everyday life. His message calls upon us to replace despair with hope, dependency with self-reliance, and empty rhetoric with meaningful action.

Iqbal’s message is not merely a part of history; it is a roadmap for the future. Honouring him means turning his vision into reality and empowering our youth to lead Pakistan towards a more enlightened, prosperous and dignified future.

AMIR SHAHZAD,

Karachi.

headline: Revisiting Iqbal Museum
description: A grateful nation observed another birth anniversary of the great thinker, philosopher and poet Dr Muhammad Iqbal on November 9, 2026, paying homage to
author: Muhammad Zahid Raffat
article_text:
A grateful nation observed another birth anniversary of the great thinker, philosopher and poet Dr Muhammad Iqbal on November 9, 2026, paying homage to his invaluable contributions towards the creation of Pakistan. Allama Iqbal awakened the Muslims of the subcontinent and, more significantly, presented the concept of a separate homeland where they could lead their lives according to their religious beliefs and enjoy social and economic freedom, free from Hindu economic domination. His vision was subsequently translated into reality by Quaid-i-Azam Muhammad Ali Jinnah through his inspiring leadership and statesmanship in a remarkably short period.

Pakistan came into existence on August 14, 1947, but Allama Iqbal did not live to witness the birth of the homeland he had envisioned. He passed away on April 21, 1938, more than nine years before independence. He lies buried beside the steps of the historic Badshahi Mosque in Lahore, where his mausoleum remains a place of national reverence.

Dr Muhammad Iqbal breathed his last at Javed Manzil, the residence he had constructed in the name of his younger son, Javed Iqbal. The historic building has since been converted into the Iqbal Museum, preserving his personal belongings, handwritten manuscripts, books and numerous articles of daily use. These possessions offer visitors a rare glimpse into the personal and intellectual life of the great philosopher and poet, whose literary contributions in Urdu and Persian continue to inspire generations.

It is worth mentioning that Allama Iqbal’s Persian poetry enjoys considerable popularity in neighbouring Iran. Visiting Iranian dignitaries invariably make it a point to pay homage at his mausoleum in Lahore, honouring the thinker and poet widely celebrated as the Poet of the East.

A visit to the Iqbal Museum, particularly around his birth anniversary, can therefore prove to be an enriching and informative experience for anyone interested in his life, philosophy and contributions to the Muslim world.

Before moving to Javed Manzil in May 1935, Allama Iqbal had lived at several other locations in Lahore. According to information gathered from various sources, following his return from Germany, he resided at different times between 1906 and 1935 in an upper storey above the premises of Attar Chand Kapur Booksellers in Anarkali, on McLeod Road and at a residence inside Bhati Gate.

The construction and ownership of Javed Manzil, situated along the road connecting Lahore Railway Station with Garhi Shahu, now known as Allama Iqbal Road, make for particularly interesting reading, especially for scholars engaged in Iqbal studies, or Iqbaliyat.

While living in rented accommodation on McLeod Road, Allama Iqbal purchased a seven-kanal plot of land in Mauza Garhi Shahu through an open auction in 1934. The property was registered in the name of his son, Javed Iqbal. Construction of the residence was completed at a cost of Rs42,025, and Allama Iqbal moved there in May 1935.

Interestingly, he rented three front rooms from his son for his own use at a monthly rent of Rs50. The written rental agreement, or karaya namah, remains preserved in the museum alongside several other documents. This reflects Allama Iqbal’s meticulous habit of recording transactions in writing, leaving behind valuable documentary evidence for future generations.

During his relatively brief stay at Javed Manzil, Allama Iqbal received several distinguished visitors, including Quaid-i-Azam Muhammad Ali Jinnah and his sister Fatima Jinnah in 1936. Among his other visitors was the prominent Hindu leader Pandit Jawaharlal Nehru, who was himself a great admirer of Iqbal’s poetry and intellectual achievements.

However, within days of moving into his newly constructed residence, Allama Iqbal suffered a profound personal loss. His wife, Sardar Begum, the mother of Javed Iqbal, passed away on May 24, 1935.

Allama Iqbal was born on November 9, 1877, into a Kashmiri family headed by Sheikh Noor Muhammad in Kashmiri Mohallah, Sialkot. His birthplace, now known as Iqbal Manzil, had been purchased by his grandfather, Sheikh Muhammad Rafiq, in 1861.

His date of birth was officially confirmed following extensive research conducted by the National Committee for Birth Centenary Celebrations, established by then Prime Minister Zulfikar Ali Bhutto. Bhutto himself visited Allama Iqbal’s mausoleum on January 1, 1977, to inaugurate the year-long centenary celebrations.

The committee also recommended that the federal government acquire Javed Manzil and convert it into a museum where Allama Iqbal’s personal belongings, manuscripts and other possessions could be preserved and displayed for posterity.

On the persuasion of General Muhammad Ziaul Haq, the property’s owner, Justice (retd) Dr Javed Iqbal, agreed to sell Javed Manzil, along with his father’s belongings, to the federal government for Rs3.5 million.

The federal government took possession of Javed Manzil in December 1977, initiating its transformation into the Iqbal Museum. The museum was initially inaugurated on December 2, 1977, by General Muhammad Ziaul Haq, then President and Chief of Army Staff. Following further renovation work, undertaken with the assistance of Japanese engineers who had specially visited Lahore at the invitation of the federal government, the museum was inaugurated again in December 1984.

Since the centenary celebrations, November 9 has been officially commemorated as Allama Iqbal’s birth anniversary, both nationally and internationally. A ceremonial changing of the guard takes place at his mausoleum in Lahore, alongside numerous official and public functions paying tribute to his life and achievements.

His death anniversary is similarly observed every year on April 21 with due respect and reverence. Literary gatherings, seminars and commemorative events recall his services towards the creation of a separate homeland for the Muslims of the subcontinent, as well as his remarkable contributions to literature, poetry and philosophy.

During the final years of General Pervez Musharraf’s tenure, approximately 50 articles displayed at the Iqbal Museum were transferred to Islamabad on his instructions. These were subsequently placed on display at the newly established National Monument Museum.

When contacted a couple of years ago, the curator of the Iqbal Museum, Dr Rustam Khan, informed this writer that none of these items had been returned. He nevertheless maintained that their continued display in Islamabad served a useful purpose, as they were appropriately preserved and presented to visitors at the National Monument Museum.

According to him, the exhibits attracted considerable interest from visitors who wished to learn about Allama Iqbal’s personal life but could not necessarily travel from Islamabad to Lahore to visit the original museum. Their presence in the capital thus provided another opportunity for the public to appreciate the poet’s legacy.

A library and an auditorium have also been added to the Iqbal Museum. The library was being developed to house books by and about Allama Iqbal, particularly for the benefit of visitors and research scholars seeking a deeper understanding of his literary and philosophical contributions.

Following the sale of Javed Manzil, Justice (retd) Dr Javed Iqbal moved to a bungalow of his choice on Main Boulevard, Gulberg, Lahore, where he spent his later years and eventually passed away.

One of the rooms in his Gulberg residence houses an impressive mural inspired by Allama Iqbal’s celebrated poetic masterpiece, Javed Namah. The mural was created by prominent Pakistani artist Jimmy Engineer at the invitation of Dr Javed Iqbal. The artist completed the challenging undertaking over approximately one year, between 1980 and 1981, during which he also stayed at the residence.

Interestingly, Allama Iqbal had reportedly expressed in one of his letters to his son Javed Iqbal the belief that translating Javed Namah into a painting or mural would be an extraordinarily difficult artistic task. He suggested that whoever succeeded in accomplishing it would achieve international recognition and fame.

Jimmy Engineer takes considerable and justified pride in having completed this demanding project, which several other Pakistani and foreign artists had reportedly attempted over the years without success. His work remains a remarkable artistic interpretation of Allama Iqbal’s philosophical imagination.

The Iqbal Museum, however, deserves much greater attention than it presently receives. Research scholars, particularly those specialising in Iqbaliyat, should visit it more frequently to examine the invaluable material preserved within its walls.

Despite offering free entry, the museum does not attract the number of visitors one might reasonably expect, whether from the general public, students or serious researchers. This is unfortunate, considering the historical, literary and educational importance of the collection.

On display are Allama Iqbal’s personal belongings, books, utensils, clothing, handwritten manuscripts in Urdu and Persian, correspondence and numerous other objects associated with his daily life. Each exhibit offers an opportunity to understand another dimension of the man whose ideas helped shape the destiny of the Muslims of the subcontinent.

There is much more to discover at the Iqbal Museum than can be covered in this brief account. A visit offers an opportunity to move beyond ceremonial tributes and familiar quotations, and engage more closely with the personal life, intellectual journey and enduring literary and philosophical contributions of one of the greatest thinkers produced by the Muslim world.

The museum stands as a valuable repository of our national and intellectual heritage. It deserves to be explored, appreciated and preserved with the seriousness that Allama Iqbal’s legacy demands.

A visit to the Iqbal Museum would be a fitting tribute to the great thinker and poet, and an opportunity to discover how much more there remains to learn about his extraordinary life.

Muhammad Zahid Rifat The writer is Lahore-based Freelance Journalist, Columnist and retired Deputy Controller (News), Radio Pakistan, Islamabad and can be reached at zahidriffat@gmail.com

article_html:
A grateful nation observed another birth anniversary of the great thinker, philosopher and poet Dr Muhammad Iqbal on November 9, 2026, paying homage to his invaluable contributions towards the creation of Pakistan. Allama Iqbal awakened the Muslims of the subcontinent and, more significantly, presented the concept of a separate homeland where they could lead their lives according to their religious beliefs and enjoy social and economic freedom, free from Hindu economic domination. His vision was subsequently translated into reality by Quaid-i-Azam Muhammad Ali Jinnah through his inspiring leadership and statesmanship in a remarkably short period.

ATC grants 13-day remand of 2 JUI-F men; party alleges harassment

Pakistan came into existence on August 14, 1947, but Allama Iqbal did not live to witness the birth of the homeland he had envisioned. He passed away on April 21, 1938, more than nine years before independence. He lies buried beside the steps of the historic Badshahi Mosque in Lahore, where his mausoleum remains a place of national reverence.

Dr Muhammad Iqbal breathed his last at Javed Manzil, the residence he had constructed in the name of his younger son, Javed Iqbal. The historic building has since been converted into the Iqbal Museum, preserving his personal belongings, handwritten manuscripts, books and numerous articles of daily use. These possessions offer visitors a rare glimpse into the personal and intellectual life of the great philosopher and poet, whose literary contributions in Urdu and Persian continue to inspire generations.

Court rejects plea to drop terrorism charge in Group Captain’s murder case

It is worth mentioning that Allama Iqbal’s Persian poetry enjoys considerable popularity in neighbouring Iran. Visiting Iranian dignitaries invariably make it a point to pay homage at his mausoleum in Lahore, honouring the thinker and poet widely celebrated as the Poet of the East.

A visit to the Iqbal Museum, particularly around his birth anniversary, can therefore prove to be an enriching and informative experience for anyone interested in his life, philosophy and contributions to the Muslim world.

Before moving to Javed Manzil in May 1935, Allama Iqbal had lived at several other locations in Lahore. According to information gathered from various sources, following his return from Germany, he resided at different times between 1906 and 1935 in an upper storey above the premises of Attar Chand Kapur Booksellers in Anarkali, on McLeod Road and at a residence inside Bhati Gate.

Senate Health Committee calls for strict enforcement of breastfeeding ordinance

The construction and ownership of Javed Manzil, situated along the road connecting Lahore Railway Station with Garhi Shahu, now known as Allama Iqbal Road, make for particularly interesting reading, especially for scholars engaged in Iqbal studies, or Iqbaliyat.

While living in rented accommodation on McLeod Road, Allama Iqbal purchased a seven-kanal plot of land in Mauza Garhi Shahu through an open auction in 1934. The property was registered in the name of his son, Javed Iqbal. Construction of the residence was completed at a cost of Rs42,025, and Allama Iqbal moved there in May 1935.

5 stolen motorcycles recovered in police crackdown in Kahuta

Interestingly, he rented three front rooms from his son for his own use at a monthly rent of Rs50. The written rental agreement, or karaya namah, remains preserved in the museum alongside several other documents. This reflects Allama Iqbal’s meticulous habit of recording transactions in writing, leaving behind valuable documentary 
evidence for future generations.

During his relatively brief stay at Javed Manzil, Allama Iqbal received several distinguished visitors, including Quaid-i-Azam Muhammad Ali Jinnah and his sister Fatima Jinnah in 1936. Among his other visitors was the prominent Hindu leader Pandit Jawaharlal Nehru, who was himself a great admirer of Iqbal’s poetry and intellectual achievements.

RWU holds 4th BASR meeting, reviews PhD, MPhil research synopses

However, within days of moving into his newly constructed residence, Allama Iqbal suffered a profound personal loss. His wife, Sardar Begum, the mother of Javed Iqbal, passed away on May 24, 1935.

Allama Iqbal was born on November 9, 1877, into a Kashmiri family headed by Sheikh Noor Muhammad in Kashmiri Mohallah, Sialkot. His birthplace, now known as Iqbal Manzil, had been purchased by his grandfather, Sheikh Muhammad Rafiq, in 1861.

His date of birth was officially confirmed following extensive research conducted by the National Committee for Birth Centenary Celebrations, established by then Prime Minister Zulfikar Ali Bhutto. Bhutto himself visited Allama Iqbal’s mausoleum on January 1, 1977, to inaugurate the year-long centenary celebrations.

The committee also recommended that the federal government acquire Javed Manzil and convert it into a museum where Allama Iqbal’s personal belongings, manuscripts and other possessions could be preserved and displayed for posterity.

On the persuasion of General Muhammad Ziaul Haq, the property’s owner, Justice (retd) Dr Javed Iqbal, agreed to sell Javed Manzil, along with his father’s belongings, to the federal government for Rs3.5 million.

The federal government took possession of Javed Manzil in December 1977, initiating its transformation into the Iqbal Museum. The museum was initially inaugurated on December 2, 1977, by General Muhammad Ziaul Haq, then President and Chief of Army Staff. Following further renovation work, undertaken with the assistance of Japanese engineers who had specially visited Lahore at the invitation of the federal government, the museum was inaugurated again in December 1984.

Since the centenary celebrations, November 9 has been officially commemorated as Allama Iqbal’s birth anniversary, both nationally and internationally. A ceremonial changing of the guard takes place at his mausoleum in Lahore, alongside numerous official and public functions paying tribute to his life and achievements.

His death anniversary is similarly observed every year on April 21 with due respect and reverence. Literary gatherings, seminars and commemorative events recall his services towards the creation of a separate homeland for the Muslims of the subcontinent, as well as his remarkable contributions to literature, poetry and philosophy.

During the final years of General Pervez Musharraf’s tenure, approximately 50 articles displayed at the Iqbal Museum were transferred to Islamabad on his instructions. These were subsequently placed on display at the newly established National Monument Museum.

When contacted a couple of years ago, the curator of the Iqbal Museum, Dr Rustam Khan, informed this writer that none of these items had been returned. He nevertheless maintained that their continued display in Islamabad served a useful purpose, as they were appropriately preserved and presented to visitors at the National Monument Museum.

According to him, the exhibits attracted considerable interest from visitors who wished to learn about Allama Iqbal’s personal life but could not necessarily travel from Islamabad to Lahore to visit the original museum. Their presence in the capital thus provided another opportunity for the public to appreciate the poet’s legacy.

A library and an auditorium have also been added to the Iqbal Museum. The library was being developed to house books by and about Allama Iqbal, particularly for the benefit of visitors and research scholars seeking a deeper understanding of his literary and philosophical contributions.

Following the sale of Javed Manzil, Justice (retd) Dr Javed Iqbal moved to a bungalow of his choice on Main Boulevard, Gulberg, Lahore, where he spent his later years and eventually passed away.

One of the rooms in his Gulberg residence houses an impressive mural inspired by Allama Iqbal’s celebrated poetic masterpiece, Javed Namah. The mural was created by prominent Pakistani artist Jimmy Engineer at the invitation of Dr Javed Iqbal. The artist completed the challenging undertaking over approximately one year, between 1980 and 1981, during which he also stayed at the residence.

Interestingly, Allama Iqbal had reportedly expressed in one of his letters to his son Javed Iqbal the belief that translating Javed Namah into a painting or mural would be an extraordinarily difficult artistic task. He suggested that whoever succeeded in accomplishing it would achieve international recognition and fame.

Jimmy Engineer takes considerable and justified pride in having completed this demanding project, which several other Pakistani and foreign artists had reportedly attempted over the years without success. His work remains a remarkable artistic interpretation of Allama Iqbal’s philosophical imagination.

The Iqbal Museum, however, deserves much greater attention than it presently receives. Research scholars, particularly those specialising in Iqbaliyat, should visit it more frequently to examine the invaluable material preserved within its walls.

Despite offering free entry, the museum does not attract the number of visitors one might reasonably expect, whether from the general public, students or serious researchers. This is unfortunate, considering the historical, literary and educational importance of the collection.

On display are Allama Iqbal’s personal belongings, books, utensils, clothing, handwritten manuscripts in Urdu and Persian, correspondence and numerous other objects associated with his daily life. Each exhibit offers an opportunity to understand another dimension of the man whose ideas helped shape the destiny of the Muslims of the subcontinent.

There is much more to discover at the Iqbal Museum than can be covered in this brief account. A visit offers an opportunity to move beyond ceremonial tributes and familiar quotations, and engage more closely with the personal life, intellectual journey and enduring literary and philosophical contributions of one of the greatest thinkers produced by the Muslim world.

The museum stands as a valuable repository of our national and intellectual heritage. It deserves to be explored, appreciated and preserved with the seriousness that Allama Iqbal’s legacy demands.

A visit to the Iqbal Museum would be a fitting tribute to the great thinker and poet, and an opportunity to discover how much more there remains to learn about his extraordinary life.

Muhammad Zahid Rifat
The writer is Lahore-based Freelance Journalist, Columnist and retired Deputy Controller (News), Radio Pakistan, Islamabad and can be reached at zahidriffat@gmail.com

headline: Growth Story & Growing Doubts

author: Dr Kamal Monnoo
article_text:
Are departing foreign investors implicitly questioning Pakistan’s willingness to undertake some key hard-nosed reforms? Ones that they opine are essential to realising their investments’ potential in Pakistan amidst an era of supply-chain constraints, especially in the South Asian and Persian Gulf peninsula? Or are they simply nervous about excessive governmental oversight and taxation, despite some unprecedented incentives on paper that, in many ways, are unique to Pakistan, in an environment where the bureaucracy has unbridled powers but the judiciary operates with little backbone? Or perhaps both?

Why these questions make good sense is that an initial analysis of the growth in corporate earnings for Q2, which ended in September, makes some pertinent revelations. Based on almost 30 results reported: a) median revenue growth is 21%; b) median operating profit growth is, on average, 31%; and c) median PAT growth is almost 30.5%. This is already on the back of a healthy performance in Q1, which ended in June. Yet, by all accounts, foreign industrial investors and foreign portfolio investors continue to exit the Pakistani market.

It is a given that Pakistan desperately needs capital to grow its economy, especially if the country is to fight poverty and post any type of meaningful growth. So, naturally, the continued flight of foreign portfolio investments is a point of concern.

One argument often given is that FPI managers (wherever they are) are rational people looking to maximise their gains and follow the money, as it were, in an objective manner. So, perhaps, thinking logically, given the rise in bond yields in the US and UK (another matter, though, is that they reflect the growing risk premium of US and UK sovereign paper), the already low relative attraction of Pakistan as an investment option has probably diminished further, especially when global and, more pertinently, our regional risks are worsening.

Further, the fact that Pakistan does not figure anywhere in investor choices involving AI, along with the steady depreciation of the rupee, could be additional contributing factors. Something that becomes even clearer if one looks at who actually gained or where these funds moved to.

So, between January and September this year, in dollar terms: 1) South Korea’s Kospi gained 72.4%; 2) Taiwan’s Taiex gained 64.5%; 3) Japan’s Nikkei gained 31.8%; and 4) India gained around 18.4%.

The trouble is that while there may be periods of attractive returns in Pakistan, what is truly required is to revisit policies based on mindlessly extracting taxes and correct the outdated mindset of boosting exports through currency devaluations.

Also, Pakistan seems to be caught in a no-man’s-land where, for financial investors, it is not cheap enough for real value gains but is not growing fast enough to attract growth investors. For manufacturing investors, it is neither competitive nor skilled enough to yield sustainable profits. We have seen that despite the current surge in corporate earnings, the beeline by MNCs to exit Pakistan remains unchanged.

We all know that each successive government in Pakistan over the last four decades has talked about reforms but never really adopted any of the key difficult ones, especially those that tend to be politically sensitive.

With an economy now quickly dismantling and both regional and global markets full of present and emerging challenges, it will be interesting to see whether the current team has the will and the mandate to correct course before it is too late!

headline: How Arab Americans Will Vote
description: On Election Day, Arab Americans will overwhelmingly vote for Democrats over Republicans running in Senate and congressional campaigns across the country. The
author: Dr. James J. Zogby
article_text:
On Election Day, Arab Americans will overwhelmingly vote for Democrats over Republicans running in Senate and congressional campaigns across the country. The actual margin is 59% for Democrats versus just 26% for Republicans. This dramatic swing back to the Democratic Party is just one of the findings of the most recent poll of Arab American voters commissioned by the Arab American Institute and conducted by John Zogby Strategies.

AAI and JZS have been polling Arab American voters for over three decades, and in all that time, the community has favoured Democrats, if only by a small margin. The Iraq War and the Bush administration’s widespread repressive policies against Arab and Muslim Americans and immigrants so significantly changed attitudes towards the two parties and their candidates that, for more than a decade and a half, Arab Americans ended up voting for Democrats by a two-to-one margin.

This changed in 2024 as a result of the Biden administration’s acquiescence to and, at times, overt support for Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza. The community was so angered by Democrats’ complicity in that war that support for Democrats declined, while Republican numbers rose. Democrats still had the edge, but in that November’s presidential election, a significant number of Arab Americans voted for third-party candidates, while many didn’t vote at all.

What accounts for the flip back towards the Democratic Party’s candidates in 2026? The recent AAI/JZS poll points to a number of factors; chief among them are the policies and behaviour of President Trump. Eighty-two per cent (82%) of Arab Americans say they have personally experienced economic hardship due to the rising costs of healthcare, utilities, groceries or gas prices. Ninety per cent (90%) say that the war in Gaza is still important in determining their vote (and will remain so as they choose a presidential candidate in 2028). More than two-thirds say they have experienced discrimination because of their heritage, and an even greater percentage fear this may increase in the future. In this context, President Trump’s anti-Muslim assault on Abdul El-Sayed, the Arab American Democratic Senate candidate in Michigan, has only added fuel to the dangerous fires of hate.

Finally, it’s important to note that, as our polling has demonstrated going back to a study issued in 2001, “What Ethnic Voters Really Think”, Arab Americans, like other ethnic immigrant communities, while holding moderate views on some cultural issues, are quite liberal when addressing economic and governmental policies. This is borne out in the most recent AAI/JZS poll, where 56% of Arab Americans say they are more aligned with the social and economic views of the Democratic Party, versus only 28% who say they feel more aligned with the Republican Party. And when asked to describe their political ideology — ranging from MAGA Republican on the right to Democratic Socialist on the left — only 18% indicate a right-leaning ideology, as opposed to 47% who are left-leaning. Thirty-one per cent (31%) describe themselves as moderate.

What is especially fascinating about the results in this poll is the extent of convergence in the views of the diverse component groups within the community. While there are some understandable variations in the responses given to a few questions, the most important demographic subgroups (Christian, Muslim; country of origin; immigrant or native US-born) all express concern about the economic situation, the war in Gaza and the fear of discrimination resulting from this election’s hateful anti-Muslim, anti-Arab hate speech.

Sectarian and national conflicts may afflict countries and regions across the Middle East, but Arab Americans have found their way to coalesce around shared heritage and issues of concern. It is this convergence that is the cornerstone of community building.

Dr. James J. Zogby The writer is the President of Arab American Institute.

The actual margin is 59% for Democrats versus just 26% for Republicans. This dramatic swing back to the Democratic Party is just one of the findings of the most recent poll of Arab American voters commissioned by the Arab American Institute and conducted by John

Zogby Strategies.

AAI and JZS have been polling Arab American voters for over three decades, and in all that time, the community has favoured Democrats, if only by a small margin. The Iraq War and the Bush administration’s widespread repressive policies against Arab and Muslim Americans and immigrants so significantly changed attitudes towards the two parties and their candidates that, for more than a decade and a half, Arab Americans ended up voting for Democrats by a two-to-one margin.

This changed in 2024 as a result of the Biden administration’s acquiescence to and, at times, overt support for Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza. The community was so angered by Democrats’ complicity in that war that support for Democrats declined, while Republican numbers rose. Democrats still had the edge, but in that November’s presidential election, a significant number of Arab Americans voted for third-party candidates, while many didn’t vote at all.

What accounts for the flip back towards the Democratic Party’s candidates in 2026? The recent AAI/JZS poll points to a number of factors; chief among them are the policies and behaviour of President Trump. Eighty-two per cent (82%) of Arab Americans say they have personally experienced economic hardship due to the rising costs of healthcare, utilities, groceries or gas prices. Ninety per cent (90%) say that the war in Gaza is still important in determining their vote (and will remain so as they choose a presidential candidate in 2028). More than two-thirds say they have experienced discrimination because of their heritage, and an even greater percentage fear this may increase in the future. In this context, President Trump’s anti-Muslim assault on Abdul El-Sayed, the Arab American Democratic Senate candidate in Michigan, has only added fuel to the dangerous fires of hate.

Finally, it’s important to note that, as our polling has demonstrated going back to a study issued in 2001, “What Ethnic Voters Really Think”, Arab Americans, like other ethnic immigrant communities, while holding moderate views on some cultural issues, are quite liberal when addressing economic and governmental policies. This is borne out in the most recent AAI/JZS poll, where 56% of Arab Americans say they are more aligned with the social and economic views of the Democratic Party, versus only 28% who say they feel more aligned with the Republican Party. And when asked to describe their political ideology — ranging from MAGA Republican on the right to Democratic Socialist on the left — only 18% indicate a right-leaning ideology, as opposed to 47% who are left-leaning. Thirty-one per cent (31%) describe themselves

as moderate.

What is especially fascinating about the results in this poll is the extent of convergence in the views of the diverse component groups within the community. While there are some understandable variations in the responses given to a few questions, the most important demographic subgroups (Christian, Muslim; country of origin; immigrant or native US-born) all express concern about the economic situation, the war in Gaza and the fear of discrimination resulting from this election’s hateful anti-Muslim, anti-Arab hate speech.

Sectarian and national conflicts may afflict countries and regions across the Middle East, but Arab Americans have found their way to coalesce around shared heritage and issues of concern. It is this convergence that is the cornerstone of community building.

Dr. James J. Zogby

The writer is the President of Arab American Institute.

headline: Washington Reengaged
description: Despite the turmoil engulfing the Middle East and growing geopolitical uncertainty, Pakistan’s relationship with the United States has improved markedly.
author: The Nation
article_text:
Despite the turmoil engulfing the Middle East and growing geopolitical uncertainty, Pakistan’s relationship with the United States has improved markedly. After years of diplomatic stagnation, particularly during the Imran Khan-Joe Biden era, Islamabad has restored engagement with Washington that once seemed increasingly elusive.

This turnaround reflects sustained diplomacy. Pakistan’s involvement in the Gaza and Iran crises, alongside carefully negotiated economic arrangements with US-linked enterprises, has helped reposition the country as a valuable regional partner. Washington is increasingly engaging with Islamabad beyond the narrow prism of Afghanistan and counterterrorism that dominated relations for decades.

The nomination of Natalie Baker as US ambassador to Pakistan is a further indication of this shift. Although Senate confirmation remains pending, nominating the incumbent chargé d’affaires signals an interest in continuity and deeper engagement.

Baker is already a familiar and well-regarded figure in Pakistan. Having arrived in Islamabad in 2024 and served as chargé d’affaires since January 2025, she has developed working relationships with the government and participated in important initiatives. Her previous assignments in Qatar, Libya, Kuwait and Iran-related diplomatic affairs provide valuable experience in a region facing considerable instability.

If confirmed, her appointment would offer Islamabad the advantage of an ambassador already acquainted with Pakistan’s institutions, political realities and strategic priorities. Such continuity could help translate improving diplomatic relations into durable economic and strategic cooperation.

Yet Pakistan must remain mindful of the wider geopolitical balance. Stronger relations with Washington should complement, rather than undermine, longstanding partnerships with China and other powers. An improvement in bilateral ties must never come at the expense of strategic independence.

In an increasingly fractured international order, diplomatic flexibility is essential. Islamabad has made progress in rebuilding ties with Washington. The challenge now is to consolidate these gains while maintaining the balanced foreign policy that Pakistan’s circumstances demand.

headline: Justice Prevails
description: In Pakistan, justice for the rich and powerful often operates differently from justice for the common citizen. Nowhere is this disparity more apparent than in
author: The Nation
article_text:
In Pakistan, justice for the rich and powerful often operates differently from justice for the common citizen. Nowhere is this disparity more apparent than in cases involving fatal road accidents, grievous bodily harm and other offences where political influence, financial resources and social standing can determine whether an accused faces punishment or walks free.

Too often, such cases disappear into a labyrinth of legal technicalities, political pressure and financial settlements. The outdated application of concepts such as blood money has frequently allowed accountability to become a transaction, particularly when the accused enjoys considerable influence. For ordinary Pakistanis, securing justice against such individuals can seem almost hopeless.

Against this backdrop, the Balochistan High Court’s decision to sentence former MPA Abdul Majeed Achakzai to ten years in prison for the death of traffic policeman Haji Attaullah is welcome.

The incident occurred in June 2017, when a speeding vehicle struck the policeman while he was performing his duty in Quetta. Despite CCTV footage and considerable public outrage, the former lawmaker was acquitted in 2020. Nearly nine years later, the High Court has overturned that acquittal and ordered his arrest.

That justice has taken almost a decade remains a serious indictment of the system. Yet the conviction demonstrates that accountability remains possible, even when the accused possesses political connections and influence.

Pakistan has witnessed far too many instances where influential defendants have escaped meaningful punishment while victims’ families were left to accept whatever settlement circumstances permitted.

This ruling must establish a precedent for how such cases are pursued and adjudicated. The stature of an accused individual, their political affiliations or financial standing must never determine the outcome of criminal proceedings.

Justice delayed remains a grave failing. But justice delivered against the powerful deserves recognition. Such outcomes must become routine rather than exceptional.

headline: Nuclear Threshold
description: Once again, the Middle East appears to be approaching war. American forces are gathering, reports of preliminary strikes on Iran’s Qeshm Island have
author: The Nation
article_text:
Once again, the Middle East appears to be approaching war. American forces are gathering, reports of preliminary strikes on Iran’s Qeshm Island have raised tensions, European governments are moving citizens out of the region, and markets are bracing for another economic shock. Even as Tehran calls for negotiations, the machinery of war appears to be moving faster than diplomacy.

Behind the prospect of renewed hostilities lies a disturbing question: could the United States use nuclear weapons against Iran’s fortified underground facilities?

A few years ago, such a possibility would have seemed unthinkable. Yet successive American and Israeli military actions have lowered the threshold of what the world considers conceivable. Nuclear use remains unlikely, but the fact that it is being discussed should alarm everyone.

The consequences would be catastrophic. A nuclear strike would not guarantee Iranian capitulation. It could instead provoke retaliation, disrupt Gulf shipping and plunge the region into an uncontrollable conflict.

For Pakistan, the danger is especially serious. Nevertheless, claims that any attack on Iranian nuclear facilities would inevitably spread radioactive fallout into Pakistan are scientifically unsound. Enrichment plants and operating nuclear reactors present different risks. Any cross-border contamination would depend on the target, weapons used, radioactive material released and prevailing winds.

Its proximity to Iran makes complacency impossible, particularly when escalation threatens lives and livelihoods.

Pakistan must prepare responsibly, with radiation monitoring, emergency planning and clear public communication, without creating unnecessary panic. Precaution is essential, but speculation cannot replace scientific assessment.

More importantly, Islamabad must use every diplomatic channel to oppose renewed hostilities and press for a negotiated settlement. The region has already suffered immeasurably from war, displacement and economic upheaval.

Even a remote possibility of nuclear escalation demands urgent action. Pakistan’s priority must be preventing a second round of war before events move beyond anyone’s control.

Once again, the Middle East appears to be approaching war. American forces are gathering, reports of preliminary strikes on Iran’s Qeshm Island have raised tensions, European governments are moving citizens out of the region, and markets are bracing for another economic shock. Even as Tehran calls for negotiations, the machinery of war appears to be moving faster than diplomacy.

Behind the prospect of renewed hostilities lies a disturbing question: could the United States use nuclear weapons against Iran’s fortified underground facilities?

ATC grants 13-day remand of 2 JUI-F men; party alleges harassment

A few years ago, such a possibility would have seemed unthinkable. Yet successive American and Israeli military actions have lowered the threshold of what the world considers conceivable. Nuclear use remains unlikely, but the fact that it is being discussed should alarm everyone.

The consequences would be catastrophic. A nuclear strike would not guarantee Iranian capitulation. It could instead provoke retaliation, disrupt Gulf shipping and plunge the region into an uncontrollable conflict.

For Pakistan, the danger is especially serious. Nevertheless, claims that any attack on Iranian nuclear facilities would inevitably spread radioactive fallout into Pakistan are scientifically unsound. Enrichment plants and operating nuclear reactors present different risks. Any cross-border contamination would depend on the target, weapons used, radioactive material released and prevailing winds.

Court rejects plea to drop terrorism charge in Group Captain’s murder case

Its proximity to Iran makes complacency impossible, particularly when escalation threatens lives and livelihoods.

Pakistan must prepare responsibly, with radiation monitoring, emergency planning and clear public communication, without creating unnecessary panic. Precaution is essential, but speculation cannot replace scientific assessment.

More importantly, Islamabad must use every diplomatic channel to oppose renewed hostilities and press for a negotiated settlement. The region has already suffered immeasurably from war, displacement and economic upheaval.

Senate Health Committee calls for strict enforcement of breastfeeding ordinance

Even a remote possibility of nuclear escalation demands urgent action. Pakistan’s priority must be preventing a second round of war before events move beyond anyone’s control.

headline: Sadiq Pashto Literary Society to elect new cabinet in January
description: Peshawar - The Sadiq Pashto Literary Society, Teri, has decided to hold elections for its new cabinet in January next year, inviting interested
author: OUR STAFF REPORT
article_text:
Peshawar - The Sadiq Pashto Literary Society, Teri, has decided to hold elections for its new cabinet in January next year, inviting interested members to submit their nomination papers to the general secretary during December.

The decision was taken at the society’s monthly meeting chaired by its President Professor Aziz Qureshi and attended by prominent poets, writers and literary figures. Renowned Pashto poet Azmat Betab attended as a special guest from Gumbat, while Kashif Karwan, an Urdu lecturer at Cadet College Teri, was the guest of honour. Advocate Usman Khattak also attended. The second session featured an open poetry recital, in which Professor Aziz Qureshi, Sarwar Mahmood Khattak, Usman Khattak, Naseer Ustad, Pervez Chambaili, Azmat Betab, Professor Shaheed Ahmad, Amal Khan Sahir, Kashif Karwan, Zeeshan Beqarar, Yar Muhammad Satori, Sehrullah Sahar and Atif Hussain Anokhi presented their poetry.

The audience warmly applauded the poets for their literary contributions.

headline: Meeting reviews effective utilization of mineral resources in KP
description: Peshawar - Adviser to the Governor of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa for Minerals, Tourism, Culture, Sports and Youth Affairs, Dr Sarfaraz Ali Shah, chaired a
author: OUR STAFF REPORT
article_text:
Peshawar - Adviser to the Governor of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa for Minerals, Tourism, Culture, Sports and Youth Affairs, Dr Sarfaraz Ali Shah, chaired a high-level meeting of the Mineral Investment Facilitation Authority (MIFA) to review key matters concerning the development of the mineral sector, improvement of the mining system, effective utilization of mineral resources and promotion of investment in the province.

The meeting was attended by the Secretary Minerals, Secretary Forests, Director General Minerals, Commissioner Mines and senior officials from the Law Department, Finance Department and other relevant departments.

Detailed discussions were held on increasing provincial revenue from the mineral sector, introducing special legislation related to mining, demarcating mining areas, addressing matters concerning Guzara Forests, formulating standard operating procedures (SOPs) for smart mining and resolving administrative and legal issues faced by the mining sector.

The participants also discussed measures to streamline and strengthen the mining sector through effective monitoring of mineral resources, transparent procedures and the use of modern technology, with the objective of maximizing the economic benefits of the province’s natural resources. In this regard, the need to formulate clear SOPs for smart mining and ensure effective coordination among the relevant departments was emphasized.

The meeting also deliberated on a proposal to establish various committees to address issues related to the mining sector.

Speaking on the occasion, Dr Sarfaraz Ali Shah said that Khyber Pakhtunkhwa was rich in natural mineral resources and that their effective utilization could strengthen the provincial economy, increase government revenue and create new investment opportunities.

He emphasized that a modern mining system, clear legislation, transparent policies and effective cooperation among all relevant institutions were essential for the sustainable development of the mineral sector.

The Adviser on Minerals urged the concerned officials to identify obstacles and challenges hindering the development of the mining sector and present concrete proposals for addressing them. He stressed the need for coordinated efforts to modernize the sector in line with contemporary requirements.

He added that the platform of the Mineral Investment Facilitation Authority (MIFA) should be effectively utilized to promote investment in the mineral sector, resolve institutional issues and take practical steps towards establishing a transparent, well-organized and investor-friendly mining system in the province.

headline: Food controller suspended over alleged wheat flour irregularities
description: Peshawar - Advisor to the Governor of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa for Home and Tribal Affairs, Food, and Women Empowerment, Kifayat Ullah Khan, has ordered
author: OUR STAFF REPORT
article_text:
Peshawar - Advisor to the Governor of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa for Home and Tribal Affairs, Food, and Women Empowerment, Kifayat Ullah Khan, has ordered the suspension of the District Food Controller, Mansehra, for three months over alleged irregularities involving government wheat flour.

He has also directed the initiation of a fact-finding inquiry to establish the facts and fix responsibility. The action follows reports of the recovery of approximately 600 bags of government wheat flour during a raid conducted by the Additional Assistant Commissioner in Mansehra district.

Taking serious notice of the reported incident, the Advisor emphasized that government wheat and subsidised flour are public resources intended solely for the relief of the people. He said that any alleged misappropriation, illegal diversion, or misuse of these resources would be dealt with strictly in accordance with the law.

The fact-finding inquiry will examine all aspects of the incident, including the roles of the concerned flour mill, dealers, and relevant field staff, to determine the circumstances and establish responsibility. The Advisor directed that the investigation be conducted transparently, impartially, and within the prescribed legal framework.

Kifayat Ullah Khan further directed the Food Department to strengthen its monitoring and enforcement mechanisms, ensure strict compliance with standard operating procedures (SOPs), and maintain effective oversight of the wheat and flour distribution system.

He reiterated that accountability, transparency, and the protection of public resources were non-negotiable priorities, adding that no negligence or malpractice would be tolerated in the distribution of subsidised flour. He stressed that the department must ensure the uninterrupted delivery of relief to its intended beneficiaries.

He has also directed the initiation of a fact-finding inquiry to establish the facts and fix responsibility. The action follows reports of the recovery of approximately 600 bags of government wheat flour during a raid conducted by the Additional Assistant Commissioner in Mansehra district.

Taking serious notice of the reported incident, the Advisor emphasized that government wheat and subsidised flour are public resources intended solely for the relief of the people. He said that any alleged misappropriation, illegal diversion, or misuse of these resources would be dealt with strictly in accordance with the law.

The fact-finding inquiry will examine all aspects of the incident, including the roles of the concerned flour mill, dealers, and relevant field staff, to determine the circumstances and establish responsibility. The Advisor directed that the investigation be conducted transparently, impartially, and within the prescribed legal framework.

Kifayat Ullah Khan further directed the Food Department to strengthen its monitoring and enforcement mechanisms, ensure strict compliance with standard operating procedures (SOPs), and maintain effective oversight of the wheat and flour distribution system.

He reiterated that accountability, transparency, and the protection of public resources were non-negotiable priorities, adding that no negligence or malpractice would be tolerated in the distribution of subsidised flour. He stressed that the department must ensure the uninterrupted delivery of relief to its intended beneficiaries.

headline: PDA directed to plant one million trees in Peshawar next spring
description: PESHAWAR - Advisor to the Governor of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa for Local Government, Communications and Works, Transport, Agriculture, and Housing,
author: OUR STAFF REPORT
article_text:
PESHAWAR - Advisor to the Governor of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa for Local Government, Communications and Works, Transport, Agriculture, and Housing, Asif Rafiq, has directed officials of the Peshawar Development Authority (PDA) to launch a plantation drive and plant one million trees across Peshawar during the coming spring season.

He also directed the authorities to formulate a comprehensive and practical plan to make the city greener and restore its identity as the “City of Flowers.” Furthermore, he instructed the relevant officials to ensure the full implementation of existing guidelines aimed at reducing traffic congestion and improving traffic flow on the city’s roads.

He issued these directives while chairing an online review meeting of the Peshawar Development Authority on Tuesday.

During the meeting, PDA officials gave a detailed briefing on ongoing public development projects, measures being taken to beautify the city, and initiatives to promote flowers and tree plantation along roads, at intersections, and in other public spaces.

Expressing satisfaction with the briefing, the Advisor directed the relevant authorities to initiate commercial activities to enhance the Authority’s revenue generation. He emphasized that all funds utilized by the Authority come from taxpayers’ money and must, therefore, be spent transparently, judiciously, and strictly in the public interest.

He also directed the authorities to plant trees along all drains across the city and organize a Spring Show during the season to promote Peshawar’s beauty and floral culture.

headline: PBC condemns police raids on homes, offices of lawyers, bar leaders
description: ISLAMABAD - The Pakistan Bar Council (PBC) has condemned the police raids at the residences and offices of Senator Kamran Murtaza, former PBC
author: OUR STAFF REPORT
article_text:
ISLAMABAD - The Pakistan Bar Council (PBC) has condemned the police raids at the residences and offices of Senator Kamran Murtaza, former PBC vice-chairman, and Aurangzeb Khan Kakar, President, Quetta Bar Association as well as other members of the legal fraternity.

In a statement, issued by the Council Secretary, Vice-Chairman Pir Muhammad Masood Chishti, Chairman Executive Committee Munir Ahmed Malik and other members of the PBC have strongly condemned the police raids at the residences and offices of Senator Kamran Murtaza, former Vice-Chairman, Pakistan Bar Council and ex-President, Supreme Court Bar Association of Pakistan and Aurangzeb Khan Kakar, President, Quetta Bar Association as well as other members of the legal fraternity.

They expressed serious concern over these incidents and termed such actions are highly unacceptable, particularly when directed against prominent members of the legal fraternity and bar leaders.

They observed that such tactics are being used as a means of political victimization and harassment, aimed at depriving individuals of their fundamental and human rights and implicating political opponents in fabricated cases. They urged the federal government, the Balochistan government and the Inspector General of Police, Balochistan, to take immediate notice, identify those responsible and initiate appropriate action against them in accordance with law.

They further emphasized that such tactics must not be repeated and the dignity, independence and respect of the legal fraternity, particularly lawyers and bar leaders, must be protected at all costs. They also warned that if such incidents are not stopped and those responsible are not held accountable, the legal fraternity will be compelled to decide its future course of action.

headline: Another Shangla labourer dies in coal mine gas incident
description: Shangla - Another young labourer from Shangla has lost his life after being exposed to poisonous gas while working in a coal mine. The incident
author: Aftab Hussain
article_text:
Shangla - Another young labourer from Shangla has lost his life after being exposed to poisonous gas while working in a coal mine. The incident occurred in Darra Adam Khel, where Bakht Zada, a resident of the remote upper area of Alandar Barbashal in Shangla, died on his very first day at work.

For the young man, who had joined the coal mining sector in search of a livelihood, his first day at work proved to be his last. His body was brought to his native village, Alandar Barbashal, on Tuesday, where he was laid to rest.

His tragic death has once again plunged the entire area into mourning and highlighted the hardships faced by labourers’ families in Shangla, as well as the urgent need to create alternative employment opportunities in the district.

According to details, Bakht Zada had travelled to Darra Adam Khel a few days earlier in search of a livelihood to earn an honest living and support his family. He had many dreams and aspirations. He wanted to support his impoverished family, educate his younger brothers and sisters, and secure a better future for them.

However, fate had other plans. On his first day underground in the coal mine, poisonous gas filled the mine, leaving him unable to make it out alive. His fellow workers tried to rescue him, but it was too late.

When news of his death reached his native village of Alandar Barbashal, a wave of grief swept across the area. His parents, brothers, sisters and other relatives were inconsolable. The young man who had left home with hopes of earning a livelihood returned in a coffin.

His funeral prayer was offered in his native village and attended by a large number of local residents, elders, young people and relatives. The participants prayed for the elevation of his ranks and for patience and strength for the bereaved family.

The incident has once again raised serious questions about safety measures in coal mines and the vulnerability of labourers from Shangla, who often work under hazardous conditions to support their families.

headline: Pakistan to establish FMD vaccine manufacturing facilities within a year
description: ISLAMABAD - Pakistan and Türkiye have agreed to strengthen cooperation in the livestock sector, focusing on Foot and Mouth Disease (FMD)
author: Farwa Naqvi
article_text:
ISLAMABAD - Pakistan and Türkiye have agreed to strengthen cooperation in the livestock sector, focusing on Foot and Mouth Disease (FMD) control, vaccine manufacturing, livestock development and meat exports.

The agreement was reached during a meeting between Federal Minister for National Food Security and Research Rana Tanveer Hussain and Türkish Minister of Agriculture and Forestry, Ibrahim Yumakli, in Türkiye.

Rana Tanveer Hussain informed his Turkish counterpart that, on the Prime Minister’s directives, Pakistan is pursuing the establishment of FMD vaccine manufacturing facilities within one year through two projects—one by the government of Punjab and the other at the federal level.

He also expressed Pakistan’s intention to export meat to Türkiye following the successful completion of the FMD-free zone project.

The two sides agreed to enhance technical cooperation by benefiting from Türkiye’s expertise in livestock development, disease control and vaccine production. The understanding follows reciprocal visits by technical delegations from both countries to assess livestock facilities, farms, slaughterhouses and vaccine manufacturing plants. The ministers expressed confidence that stronger bilateral collaboration would support Pakistan’s livestock sector and create new opportunities for agricultural trade between the two countries.

headline: Peace essential for economic growth, youth empowerment: Dr Aamer
description: Peshawar - Adviser to the Governor of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa for Education and Social Welfare, Dr Aamer Abdullah, has said that establishment of peace
author: OUR STAFF REPORT
article_text:
Peshawar - Adviser to the Governor of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa for Education and Social Welfare, Dr Aamer Abdullah, has said that establishment of peace promotes economic activity, business, livelihoods and the aspirations of young people.

He emphasized that the intellectual outlook and role of young people are vital to promoting peace, economic prosperity and positive social change. He said that youth are not merely the future of the nation but also its leaders in the present, whose ideas, capabilities and suggestions can pave the way for social reform and development.

He expressed these views while addressing the first day of a two-day Youth Engagement Workshop for young people from the merged districts in Peshawar as the chief guest.

The workshop was organized by the Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Centre for Countering Violent Extremism in collaboration with the Sustainable Social Development Organization (SSDO) and the British High Commission.

Highlighting the role of young people in bringing about social reform, Dr Aamer quoted a scholar who said that when the people of a settlement are forced to drink water from a stagnant pond, their hopes are pinned on the youth, who are expected to find a pure and fresh spring. He said this example reflected the intellectual potential, responsibility and significant role of young people in addressing societal challenges.

The Adviser for Education and Social Welfare said that the fundamental objective of the two-day workshop was to listen to the problems faced by young people in the tribal districts, their proposed solutions and their suggestions for establishing peace. He said young people were more familiar with their local needs and ground realities; therefore, their input could help formulate effective policies and address issues related to peace and development.

Referring to his visits to the tribal areas during his tenure in the previous caretaker government, Dr Aamer said he used to hold separate meetings with young people, elders and government officials. He observed that what he learned through face-to-face interactions with the youth of the tribal areas was far more valuable than all his academic and practical efforts concerning the tribal regions. He described the experience as immensely valuable.

Addressing the participants, Dr Aamer said the workshop had provided policymakers with an opportunity to learn from young people and benefit from their experiences. He expressed hope that the collaborative working groups formed during the two-day workshop would develop effective and practical recommendations. He said he would personally review the proposals to help formulate better policies in light of the recommendations.

Other speakers on the first day of the workshop included Secretary Higher Education, Archives and Libraries Abidullah Kakakhel; renowned intellectual and former Chairman of the Council of Islamic Ideology and the Federal Shariat Court, Prof. Dr Qibla Ayaz; Director of the Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Counter Violent Extremism Authority Dr Qasim Khan; Additional Director General Kashif Irshad; and Chief Executive Officer of the Sustainable Social Development Organization Kausar Abbas.
